l1: What's being built is the balance month by month: each month it earns a twelfth of the annual rate, then your deposit lands on top, $B_{n+1} = B_n\left(1 + \tfrac{r}{12}\right) + D$. You'll be able to set the starting balance, the deposit, the rate and the number of years, and add what it leaves out, like inflation or a withdrawal. The part to distrust is $r$: it's held fixed for the whole horizon, and it's the one input that's a guess about the future rather than a choice you make. Once your numbers are in, halve the rate and see how much of the final balance goes with it — that's how much of the plan is resting on the guess.

The best case on the other side: a randomized trial at Trip.com, published in Nature in 2024, found no difference in performance reviews or promotions between staff working two days a week from home and those in the office, and a third fewer of the hybrid group quit. Where losses do show up, it's mostly with fully remote work, or in the mentoring and cross-team contact that's hard to measure — real costs, but a narrower claim than the one you made. l3: *Always* is where it breaks. It's what the competitive-market model predicts, but that's one model, not all of economics: where employers have the power to set wages (monopsony), a modest minimum can raise employment. And two of the most-cited studies of real increases — Card and Krueger's New Jersey fast-food study, and a 2019 analysis of 138 US state increases — found little or no loss of jobs. The defensible version of your view is narrower: push the minimum high enough relative to local wages and losses become likely, though nobody can say exactly where that line is. What result would make you drop the "always"?
l4: "More money" is the only part of this without a number on it, and it's the part being asked to outweigh your friends — so before it gets weighed at all, it has to survive the new city's cost of living and what it costs to keep coming back. Here's a test: if the offer paid exactly what you earn now, would you still be tempted? If you would, the money isn't really what's pulling you, and it's worth knowing what is.
l5: It's the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as yours *if* the null hypothesis (usually "no effect") were true: $p = P(\text{result at least this extreme} \mid H_0)$. That "if" is where it usually gets misread: the calculation assumes nothing is going on, so it can't also tell you the chance that nothing is going on, which is why $p = 0.03$ does not mean a 3% chance the finding is a fluke. It doesn't measure the size of the effect either — with enough data, a trivially small effect gets a tiny p-value — and the 0.05 line it's usually judged against is a convention, not something anyone measured.
